title: Psalm 7: God as Our Refuge and Righteous Judge
speaker: Unknown Speaker
summary: This lesson explores Psalm 7, where David appeals to God for protection and vindication against slanderous accusations. The sermon emphasizes God's faithfulness as revealed through His covenant name Yahweh, His role as our refuge, and His position as the righteous judge who avenges His people. The message teaches believers to turn to God in times of false accusation rather than seeking self-vindication, to examine their own hearts before defending themselves, and to leave justice in God's hands.

outline.title: God's Covenant Faithfulness and the Meaning of Yahweh
subpoints: David addresses God as 'Lord, my God,' knowing Him as a covenant-keeping God
Yahweh means 'He who is'—God never changes and is always faithful
Jesus Christ is the ultimate revelation of Yahweh
God promises to never leave us or forsake us in Christ Jesus

outline.title: God as Our Refuge: Understanding David's Trust
subpoints: David's first response to persecution is to take refuge in God
God is described throughout Scripture as our hiding place, shield, and high tower
Being hidden in Christ means the Father's hand surrounds us with His protection
We must constantly turn to Christ and keep our minds upon Him

outline.title: Self-Examination Before Self-Defense
subpoints: David was willing to have God search his heart despite false accusations
He did not deny his sinful nature even when defending himself
We must examine ourselves for sin before defending ourselves against others
Apart from Christ, we are capable of committing any sin

outline.title: God as the Righteous Judge and Avenger
subpoints: God alone can determine what is truly right and wrong
God's Word is the ultimate rule for belief and conduct
Vengeance belongs to God, not to us
We must never take revenge into our own hands
God judges righteously, so we can rest in peace knowing He handles justice

outline.title: Three Practical Applications for Believers
subpoints: Run to God as your refuge when misunderstood or slandered, not to self-defense
Examine your own heart before defending yourself against accusations
Leave justice in God's hands and trust Him as the righteous judge rather than seeking revenge

transcript:
## Opening Remarks

If you know, the Psalms are my favorite book of the Bible. We're going to be reading Psalm 7.

## Scripture Reading: Psalm 7 (ESV)

A meditation of David, which he sang to the Lord concerning the words of Cush, a Benjaminite.

> O Lord, my God, in you do I take refuge; save me from all those who persecute me and deliver me, lest they tear me like a lion, rending me in pieces, with none to rescue. O Lord, my God, if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands, if I have repaid evil to him who was at peace with me or have plundered my enemy without cause, let the enemy pursue me and overtake me, and let him trample my life to the earth and lay my honor in the dust. Arise, O Lord, in your anger; lift yourself up because of the rage of my enemies; rise up for me to the judgment you have appointed. Let the congregation of the peoples be gathered about you; and over it return on high. The Lord judges the peoples; judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness and according to my integrity within me. Oh, let the wickedness of the wicked come to an end, but establish the just, for the righteous God tests the hearts and minds. My defense is of God, who saves the upright in heart. God is a just judge, and God is angry with the wicked every day. If he does not turn back, he will sharpen his sword; he bends his bow and makes it ready. He has prepared his deadly weapons, making his arrows fiery shafts. Behold, the wicked brings forth iniquity; yes, he conceives trouble and brings forth falsehood. He made a pit and dug it out and has fallen into the ditch which he made. His trouble shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealings shall come down on his own crown. I will praise the Lord according to his righteousness and will sing praise to the name of the Lord most high. (Psalm 7:1-17)

## The Context and Structure of Psalm 7

When we read this Psalm and think about it, we realize that this is probably not the kind of song we would compose about God. We wouldn't put in talk of anger, God's righteousness, and so on. But in this seventh Psalm, we note that slanderous charges had been brought against David, the king. David is upset that his honor has been questioned. So he calls God to be the judge of his character and actions.

The title tells us something peculiar about this song. Notice that it doesn't say he wrote this for the chief musician—he didn't write this for somebody else to sing. He wrote it for himself to sing. These are the words of David, sung by David to God.

It also tells us that accusations were brought against him by Cush the Benjaminite. Do you know where in the Bible we read about Cush the Benjaminite? Nowhere. It's not in the Bible. We don't have the account of what is going on here. This tells us that there are things that God chose not to include in the Bible. We don't have everything that happened in the history of the people of God in the Bible.

I point this out simply to emphasize that when we study the Bible, we need to do so with the understanding that God has a reason for everything that is in the Bible. We need to be asking ourselves: Why this, not that? Why did God choose to put these things that we have in the Bible, not some other things? Because he has a reason for everything that's included in his book.

Each biblical writer, as he was guided by the Holy Spirit, had a purpose in writing what he did. We have to remember that the Bible is not the thoughtless rumblings of man, nor is it just an objective stating of facts. If we read it thinking that it is just a truthful and accurate record of historical events—which it is—we will miss the richness of its theological and theocentric contents. The Bible is always telling something about us, about God, pointing us to Christ. There's always theology in everything that the Bible says.

There's a reason why the story of Cush is not included in the historical books, but it is here included in the title of the Psalm.

## The Appeal for Divine Protection and Vindication (Verses 1-5)

In the first five verses, we see that David, who sees himself as innocent, appeals for divine protection and vindication.

I'm not brave enough to make some of the statements that David makes here. Now he knew by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit that it was true. But I don't know that I would have the confidence to come before God at any time and say, "Judge me according to my righteousness." Does it make sense to you guys? It's just foreign to me. And yet David is able to do that in this particular instance. He's not saying he's perfect. In this accusation that Cush is bringing against him, he is innocent.

In a sense, reading this Psalm is like listening to one side of a phone conversation, where you don't know what the other side is saying. We don't know what the accusation that Cush brought against him is. We just know that he did, and that now David is talking to God about this conversation. The only thing that we know is that the accusation was a serious one, and David's soul was in anguish because of it. And in his innocence, in his indignation, David turns to the Lord for relief.

### The Meaning of "Lord, My God"

Look at verse one: "Oh Lord, my God in you, I put my trust, save me from all those who persecute me and deliver me."

Notice how David addresses God. Right there in verse one, he says "Lord, my God." God wasn't just God. To David, God was David's God. David knew God as his Father, the one who could help him, comfort him, and deliver him. He also knew that his God was the covenant-keeping God, that would always be faithful to the promises he made to his children. We see this just like we saw this morning in David calling God by his covenant name Yahweh. "Oh Yahweh, my God."

God had promised David that his covenantal faithfulness would never depart from him. In Psalm 89, which is a retelling of 2 Samuel 7, the Psalmist says, speaking on behalf of God:

> Nevertheless, my loving kindness I will not utterly take from him, from David, nor allow my faithfulness to fail. My covenant I will not break nor alter the word that has gone out of my lips. Once I have sworn by my holiness, I will not lie to David.

David knew that the God he was praying to, the God he was asking to vindicate him, was a faithful God that was not going to turn away from him.

### The Meaning of Yahweh

The very name that God chose to reveal himself by shows David that the only thing to do during this time of severe trial is to turn to God. It's interesting that Yahweh—the word Yahweh means "he who is." Some scholars have tried to make it "he who will be," but that's not really what God meant by that. He means "he who is," and the idea is that he always is. Do you understand the consequence of this thought? That God always is. There's never a time where he's not who he is. He doesn't change, he doesn't grow, he is perfect all the time.

Isn't it exactly what the writer of Hebrews told us about the Lord Jesus Christ? Remember what the Holy Spirit through the author of Hebrews in Hebrews 13:8 says?

> Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and forever.

Jesus Christ is the one who was, who is, and who is to come, which is exactly what the book of Revelation tells us about Jesus. When we mesh all that together, guess what word we come up with? Yahweh. Jesus Christ is the ultimate revelation of Yahweh. And that's why we cannot know God apart from knowing him through Jesus Christ.

And that's why the writer of Hebrews can also say that God will never leave us, nor forsake us, and that the Lord is our helper and we will not fear what comes to us—as he quotes from Psalm 27.

Now it is good for us to stop here for a moment and be reminded that we serve the same God as David. I think sometimes we read the Bible and we think, "Oh man, that was so great for those people," and you forget that the same God who is then is now. And we're serving that same God. All the things that are true about David's God are true about our God. There's not different gods out there—that's the only true God.

Our God has promised to be a God to us and to our children, as he did to David. He has promised that he's not going to leave us nor forsake us. He has promised that even when the closest earthly relationships, such as a father or mother, fail us, God in Christ Jesus will not fail us ever. His mercies, his promises are new to us every morning because he is faithful. He says that even when we are unfaithful to him, he remains faithful to us because he cannot be unfaithful. Can you believe that? Can you understand? Do you believe that, people?

That if you believe in Jesus Christ, even in your worst day full of sin, God does not turn his back on you. You cannot get him to do that. You just can't, because he remains faithful to the promise to be your God in Jesus Christ.

Knowing that this is his God, David puts his trust in him. Look at verse one. He says: "in you do I take refuge." A better translation of this Hebrew expression would be, "In you do I take refuge." That's where he's going for refuge.

### God as Our Refuge

We find this idea expressed in Psalm 5 where David says in verse 12:

> For you, O Lord, will bless the righteous; with favor you surround him as with a shield.

We find this throughout the Psalms—that God is David's refuge or the believer's refuge. In Psalm 91, verse 4, he says:

> He shall cover you with his feathers, and under his wings you shall take refuge; his truth shall be your shield and your buckler.

In Psalm 32, verse 7:

> You are my hiding place; you shall preserve me from trouble; you shall surround me with songs of deliverance.

In Psalm 119, verse 114:

> You are my hiding place and my shield; I open in your word.

And how many times we have the reference that God is our high tower, a rock of refuge. David knew God as that, so he fled to him. And this expression conveys the idea of going to a safe place when everything around you is crumbling. The enemies are attacking from every side. The battle seems to be lost and death is imminent. And then you look up and see a hiding place where nobody can harm you or touch you, and you go there.

Like I said this morning, for me when I was young my refuge was my thin little sheet over me. False hope. Yet our God is truly our refuge. That was true of David and it's as true of us.

We are often surrounded by enemies. The world, the devil, and the flesh are real enemies and they are after us. Life seems to be so full of despair. Sin seems to overcome us often. So we cry out with Paul, "Who will deliver me from the body of this death?" You know what the answer is? The same as Paul arrived at: "Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord"—because he is our refuge.

Brothers and sisters, the New Testament speaks of our lives as being hidden in Christ and in the Father. In Colossians chapter 3, there's this expression and the image that Paul is trying to get across. Using metaphorical language, not literal language, Christ has his hand around us, and then the Father comes and puts his hand around Christ's hand. And nothing can get us out of his hand. Because of that, nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus. We see that in Romans 8, verses 31 through 39.

Who is the biggest enemy of your faith? You are yourself. We are our worst enemy. And yet Paul says that even ourselves cannot separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus. As long as God is on his throne and as long as Christ is ruling over his church, we have a hiding place in him and we don't have to fear our enemies.

Is there anybody here who read the book "The Hiding Place"? You know the story with those people—whose name escapes me. Not Corrie ten Boom. Oh, Anne Frank. Yes. You read the story and the hiding place for Anne Frank was not very good, right? They had to hide behind a wall in the attic. There's not much place where they could go out. They could not look out the window for years while they were there until the Nazis came and found them. That's not Christ. We're hidden in him. He's our refuge, and yet we have pleasures forevermore. As Psalm 16, verse 11 says, because at the right hand of the Father is Jesus Christ, and he is pleasures forevermore. We're hidden in him, and yet the world is our playground. So it's a great place to hide.

However, this takes constant turning to him and keeping our minds upon him.

### Enemies as Lions

David understood that unless God intervened, his enemies would tear him like a lion would tear up his prey. So in verse 2, it says:

> Lest they tear me like a lion, rending me in pieces, with none to rescue.

I think we all feel like David at times. The affairs of life are too great to deal with. It feels like we are going to pop because things are just overwhelming and pressing from all directions.

I remember feeling like that as a teenager in high school. Things were changing very fast. I went from a 21-student eighth grade class to a thousand-student freshman class. We had, I think, eight rooms of freshmen with 60 to 70 students in each room when I first started as a freshman. Things were changing fast. There was so much pressure to conform to the group. And at the time, I had nowhere to turn for refuge.

I hope you teenagers realize this: You do have a refuge, and that refuge is Jesus Christ. And if you look for refuge somewhere else, it's like you trying to cover yourself with that thin little sheet that does nothing for you.

What a mercy that God has shown to you teenagers, that from this young age you know who your refuge is. That you can turn to him, hide yourself in him. That you don't have to find hope or refuge in the things of the world, even though sometimes you try to, but you can find refuge in Jesus Christ and in him alone. Count that as a blessing that comes from your covenant Father who told your parents, "I'm your God, but I'm also the God of your children." And you are the fulfillment of that promise.

You want evidence that God is real? You are here. And if you don't want to see, if you don't see that, open your eyes to see Christ who is your refuge, and you are the very promise of God fulfilled.

## Self-Examination Before Self-Defense (Verses 3-5)

David gives us a glimpse into what the accusations may have been and who was bringing them in verses 3 through 5. He says:

> O Lord, my God, if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands, if I have repaid evil to him who was at peace with me, or have plundered my enemy without cause, let the enemy pursue me and overtake me. Yes, let him trample my life to the earth and lay my honor in the dust.

Verse 4 tells us that not only those who were his open enemies were turning on him, but also those who were his friends—him who was at peace. The ESV translates that as "those were my friends." That's an interpretation. Literally, it's "him who was at peace."

David asks God to judge him. "You decide who is right, God. You decide. You be the judge." And David is pretty sure that he did not do anything wrong in this matter, but he knows that he's a sinner and does not put it beneath him to have done the things that he's accused of. So he says, "Lord, you judge. You look into my heart. You figure out whether I'm guilty of this or not."

In another Psalm, as we saw this morning, he says:

> Search me, O God, and know my heart; try me, and know my anxieties.

I've said this before, but it's worth repeating. Robert Murray McCheyne was a pastor in Dundee, Scotland—a very godly man. You read what he did in his life. He died at a ripe old age... well, he died at age 29 of tuberculosis, or "consumption" as they called it back then. He corresponded with his congregation, and a woman in the congregation wrote to him and said, "Pastor, I wish I was as godly as you are." And he writes back, "Madam, the seed of every sin dwells in my heart."

Brothers and sisters, apart from Christ, we are capable of doing the most heinous thing there is to do. Never put this beyond you. Never put it beyond you to do these things. It is by the grace of God that we go.

David realized that, so he asked God, "You search my heart. You prove whether I am innocent or not." In essence, David's doing what Jesus commands all of us to do in Matthew 7. "Lord, if there's a log in my eye, you take it out, that I might see my sin more clearly."

Isn't it interesting that when the sin of others calls David's attention, he asks God to purify him of his own sins instead of focusing on the sins of others. He says, "David, Lord, please start with my own heart. Let me see if I have sin here in this. Let me see if these accusations are true," instead of completely just right off the bat denying that there is any issues with him.

And if God finds him guilty, he welcomes the punishment, because he knows that God chastens those whom he loves. And to go unchastened would be to go unloved.

## Divine Justice: The Righteous Judge and Avenger (Verses 6-10)

Then David cries out for divine justice in verses 6 through 10.

After searching his heart, David found himself innocent of the charges that were brought against him. So he asks God to judge the wicked and the righteous.

The first thing we see here is that David recognized that God is the righteous judge. In verse 11, he says:

> God is a just judge, and God is angry with the wicked every day.

God is the only one who can truly determine what is right and what is wrong. As a righteous judge, he has revealed to us in his word what is right and what's wrong. Therefore, his word must be the ultimate rule for what we do and what we believe.

We also see here that David recognized that God is the Avenger of the righteous, not the righteous themselves. In verse 9, he says:

> Oh, let the wickedness of the wicked come to an end, but establish the just, for the righteous God tests the hearts and minds.

It is God who does it. It is God who avenges. Isn't that what the apostle tells us?

> Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God; for it is written, "Vengeance is mine, I will repay," says the Lord. (Romans 12:19)

The Lord is the Avenger.

Remember, we have a pastor in our present area that, when it comes to examination of candidates to the ministry, we know he's going to ask one question. He asks many questions, but there's one specific one he's going to ask. He asks about the cities of refuge and why they're there.

Do you remember the story of the cities of refuge? If you committed a capital crime—if you killed somebody—you needed a trial, so you had to run to a city of refuge. But if the relative of the deceased caught you on the way, they could kill you, because they are the kinsman redeemer. They're going to redeem the family member that was dead.

Guess who is our kinsman? Guess who is going to avenge us? Not us, but God himself, in the person of his son.

We also see here that we are not in charge of judging people to determine if we should destroy them or not. Yet it's so foreign to what we do, isn't it? Somebody offends us and the first thing in our hearts is hatred towards them or anger, which is in essence a desire to destroy them. And yet here, David says no—it is God who avenges.

And we also see that God will judge righteously. So we can rest in peace. Somebody offends us, somebody sins against us, we give it to God and we know he's going to do the best job in doing that. So we can just let it go and rest that our Lord is going to do that.

## How Shall We Then Live?

We don't want to just be hearers of the word; we want to be doers of the word, as James calls us to be. Let me give you three suggestions from this Psalm.

### First: Run to God as Your Refuge

When you are misunderstood, when you are slandered, instead of trying to vindicate yourself, run to God as your refuge. David's instinct was to go to God. David's instinct under false accusations was not self-defense, but God-dependence.

### Second: Examine Your Heart Before You Defend Yourself

David was willing to be searched by God and even punished if he were guilty. Before we defend ourselves against accusations, we should ask God to search our hearts and examine us.

### Third: Leave Justice in God's Hands

David entrusted judgment to God, recognizing him as the righteous judge. Instead of taking revenge, we should leave justice in God's hands.

And as you do that, you will make David's words yours in verse 17, where it says:

> I will praise the Lord according to his righteousness, and I will sing praise to the name of the Lord, most high.
